paras: The lynching of Charles Jones took place at Spadra, Johnson County, Arkansas, on Monday, October 31, 1881, when a mob took Jones, a Black man accused of attempting to rape a white woman, from an officer at the railroad depot and hanged him to a tree. Jones was hanged within twenty minutes of arriving at Spadra, after what the wire called a "short informal examination by a jury." A Little Rock dispatch carried the story across the country, where papers ran it under headlines such as "Speedy Justice" and "Judge Lynch's Court in Arkansas."

According to the Little Rock wire, Jones was an escaped convict who was accused of trying to rape a white woman named Mrs. Lewis near Spadra, on the Fort Smith railroad, the week before. The wire said her screams drew neighbors and that he fled, while a special to the Memphis Appeal dated the alleged attempt to "last Tuesday." Other reports described the accusation differently: one Little Rock brief said only that he had "insulted a white woman," and a syndicated digest said he had committed "an indecent assault upon a respectable white married lady."
Jones was captured at Fort Smith and brought back to Spadra by train in the charge of an officer.

A mob of 100 men armed with shotguns waited at the Spadra depot, and when the train arrived they took the prisoner from the officer. After a mock examination by a "jury," the mob condemned Jones to death and hanged him to a tree twenty minutes after his arrival. The Memphis Appeal's correspondent wrote that Jones arrived at 10 o'clock and that "the citizens of the town" escorted him to the woods, so he was taken from the depot to the woods to be hanged. The Russellville Democrat, an Arkansas weekly, reported that the hanging took place at Spadra "last Monday morning."

The coverage does not report an inquest, any arrest of mob members, or the names of anyone in the mob. A week later the Memphis Appeal's Arkansas column noted only that a Black man had been "hanged for rape by Judge Lynch" near Spadra the Monday before.

The only coverage found is in white newspapers, nearly all of it drawn from a Little Rock dispatch datelined October 31 and printed from November 1. The Chicago Tribune ran the full wire under the headline "Speedy Justice," presenting the alleged attempted rape as fact, and the St. Paul Daily Globe printed the same text as "Judge Lynch's Court in Arkansas." Shorter versions appeared in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, the Los Angeles Herald ("Swift Distribution") and the Dallas Daily Herald, and the wire was still being reprinted in South Carolina on November 10 as "Arkansas Lynching."

The Memphis Public Ledger treated the killing as a joke, calling the mob "a large committee of gentlemen" and adding that "the rope stood the jerk nobly, and is as good as new." A syndicated news digest, printed in the Batesville Guard and the Iola Register, called the woman "respectable" and stated the alleged assault as fact. The one nearby Arkansas report found, in the Russellville Democrat, was a single sentence that did not name Jones. Weekly digests also garbled the facts, as when the South Kentuckian named the victim "Chas. James" and placed the lynching "at Little Rock," the wire's dateline.

Accounts differ on where Jones was seized: the Little Rock wire said a mob took him from an officer at the depot, while a brief in the Washington Evening Critic said he was "taken from jail." The depot version is the more detailed and more widely printed, and it fits the Memphis special's account of his arrival by train. The time also varies, with the Memphis special and the Russellville Democrat placing the hanging in the morning and the wire saying he was brought to Spadra in the afternoon.
